answer: In fact, if you do sell outside your core niche, at least be honest and upfront with them about it. Tell them why you are going after that segment, what you think will work for this customer base, and how you’ll staff up more quickly once you get bigger. I’ve seen folks go from zero percent market share in one vertical to 40% market share just by being good enough, local, and responsive (i.e., better than anyone else). So even in tiny niches, there’s still room. Even with only 2 or 3 customers in a small space. But whatever you do, don’t pretend. Don’t claim to have something in a vertical where you don’t yet. And also, understand that as soon as you can pull off a $1m+ deal … you may well need someone on the team that is experienced at selling and supporting a large enterprise. Maybe not today. But pretty darn soon. That doesn’t mean you should hire them tomorrow. It means you should start recruiting for this role right now. And when you finally land that $1m+ deal, she/he might already be ready. Just like Salesforce was when they landed their first big enterprise customer. Or maybe earlier. answer: How To Truly Stand Out In An Interview (Updated) If you want to truly stand out during an interview — do something that isn’t done often enough. Especially for entry-level and mid-pack candidates. Do it right before the interview starts. I’ve been hiring since 2005 now, and what I can tell you is almost no one does this. Almost every candidate comes into an interview without any prior research on the company or role at all. Even worse, they haven’t prepared how their skills match up to the job description. That’s easy to fix with some simple homework. The best thing you can do pre-interview … is send over some notes saying you did your homework, you know where you’d like to fit on the org chart, and how you would add value as early as Week 1. It works. And it shows you are serious and willing to put in work beforehand. This will likely increase the odds you get the offer by 50% right there. At least if the other applicants don’t bother doing the same level of prep. Don’t expect anyone to care much if you didn’t do the basic research on them first. Send over those “Notes” after you schedule but before the meeting, with a few thoughts on why you think you might be a good fit. You’ll stand out already then. Now if you really want to impress someone? Add a comment or two on exactly how you plan to contribute in the first week. What you’re going to do, not just talk about it. Then the interviewer knows you aren’t just another applicant, you have real ideas on how to help. They may even be able to use you earlier than expected! So take 15-30 minutes to write down who you are, and how you could make the organization better. Not generic stuff, but specific things you can do to improve it immediately.

Fourth, reset your model. Your burn rate doesn't matter all that much once you raise millions and tens of millions in venture capital. But you will run out of money eventually. Plan on it. Fifth, finally go long. Many founders don’t really want to be CEOs forever. That makes sense.

answer: Dear SaaStr: At What Stage Should a Startup Hire a CMO? There’s no one-size-fits-all answer to this question, but here are some general guidelines based on what I’ve seen work well at startups. Early Stage (Pre-$10M ARR) : If you’re under $5M ARR and still figuring out your market positioning, don’t hire a CMO yet. Instead, focus on hiring a VP of Marketing or even just an individual contributor marketer who can help with content creation, lead generation, and early demand gen efforts. They should be able to handle most marketing tasks up to around $1-2M ARR before needing more specialized support. Around $1-2M ARR : By this point, you’ll need someone who can scale your marketing efforts as you start growing faster. This is when you might hire a Director of Demand Gen or Growth who reports directly to you, the CEO. Their job will be to create repeatable processes for generating leads and scaling your growth engine. Post-$10M ARR (Scaling Phase) : Once you hit $20-30M+ ARR, it’s time to bring in a full-time Chief Marketing Officer (CMO). A great CMO should have experience building go-to-market strategies that drive efficiency, scalability, and customer acquisition across all channels—whether it’s digital marketing, events, field sales, or product-led growth. Key characteristics of a successful CMO at this stage include: Deep industry expertise in your vertical Strong leadership skills Ability to scale teams and processes Experience managing complex marketing funnels And they should report directly to you, not any other executive unless you’re really big.

Don’t spend more than 100% of what you take home. Your personal financial health directly impacts your ability to keep funding the business.
